section_summary: This section concludes Embassy despatch No. 4324 with an analysis of Japan’s unsuccessful efforts to restrain wartime prices, mounting currency inflation, government borrowing difficulties, hoarding, speculation, and the movement toward a more comprehensively controlled economy. Six enclosures reproduce five October 1939 imperial ordinances controlling prices, wages, company remuneration, rents, and electric power, followed by a Central Price Committee list of commodities subject to price control. Together the documents show the Japanese government using the National General Mobilization Law to regulate economic activity in Japan and its colonial territories during the war in China.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4324 on Japanese price controls and the danger of inflation
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The concluding portion assesses Japan’s October 1939 price-control program and the wider inflationary pressures affecting its wartime economy.
subfiles.summary: Official and agreed prices failed to prevent wholesale and retail prices from rising, while hoarding, speculation, and reluctance to sell impeded commodity distribution despite the absence of acute general shortages. The despatch identifies rapid fiduciary-note expansion, difficulty absorbing government bonds, increased industrial lending, and a bullish stock market as danger signals. It describes government responses including credit restrictions, higher taxes, a restrained budget, enforcement against undercover trading, and the Price Control Cooperation Society. Grew concludes that price legislation forms the capstone of an increasingly controlled economy likely to require still more permanent and drastic regulation.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1: Imperial Ordinance No. 703 Concerning the Control of Prices and Other Matters
subfiles.from: Imperial Japanese Government; translated by the American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State as enclosure to despatch No. 4324
subfiles.about: The ordinance establishes ceilings and administrative controls for commodity prices, freight, storage, insurance, rents, and manufacturing charges.
subfiles.summary: Prices and related charges were generally limited to their September 18, 1939 levels, subject to administrative permission, officially approved industry agreements, and specified exceptions. Government authorities could lower unfair prices, prescribe other maximums, demand cost calculations and reports, and inspect commercial premises and records. The ordinance allocated jurisdiction among ministries and colonial administrations, exempted certain exchange and foreign-trade transactions, and replaced numerous earlier price-control regulations. Its principal controls took effect in October 1939 and were generally valid through October 19, 1940.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2: Imperial Ordinance No. 705 Relating to the Temporary Restriction of Wages
subfiles.from: Imperial Japanese Government; translated by the American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State as enclosure to despatch No. 4324
subfiles.about: The ordinance freezes and regulates wages, wage standards, increases, and bonuses across a wide range of industries.
subfiles.summary: Employers were generally prohibited from raising basic allowances or wage standards above those effective on September 18, 1939 without official authorization. Employers had to report wage schedules and wage-increase rules, while prefectural governors could revise unsuitable schedules and regulate day labor through wage committees. Separate provisions governed bonuses, inspections, seamen, mining, and the colonial territories. The measure took effect on October 20 in Japan proper and October 27 in Chosen, Taiwan, Karafuto, and the South Sea Islands, and remained valid through October 19, 1940.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 3: Imperial Ordinance No. 706 Relating to the Temporary Restriction of Allowances to Employees of Companies
subfiles.from: Imperial Japanese Government; translated by the American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State as enclosure to despatch No. 4324
subfiles.about: The ordinance restricts salaries, allowances, bonuses, and other remuneration paid to company officials and employees.
subfiles.summary: The measure applied principally to companies capitalized at ¥200,000 or more and froze remuneration under salary and allowance rules effective September 18, 1939 unless ministerial permission was obtained. It prescribed limits and reporting requirements for periodic bonuses and extraordinary allowances and authorized inspection of offices, factories, workshops, ships, accounts, and documents. Jurisdiction was divided among the finance, commerce, communications, and railways ministries, with special provisions for seamen and colonial administrations. The ordinance was effective from October 1939 through October 19, 1940.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 4: Imperial Ordinance No. 704 Relating to the Control of Ground Rent and House Rent
subfiles.from: Imperial Japanese Government; translated by the American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State as enclosure to despatch No. 4324
subfiles.about: The ordinance limits ground and house rents and regulates deposits, repair charges, and related tenancy conditions.
subfiles.summary: Owners generally could not charge more than the rent effective on August 4, 1938, or the earliest applicable later rent, unless a prefectural governor granted permission. Governors could reduce unfair rents through deliberative committees, investigate leases, and prevent lessors from evading the controls through collateral charges. Special benchmark dates and administrative arrangements applied in Chosen, Taiwan, Karafuto, and the South Sea Islands. The supplementary rules required certain excessive rents to be restored after November 1, 1939 while preserving specified court-approved or pending adjustments.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 5: Imperial Ordinance No. 708 Concerning the Control of Electric Power
subfiles.from: Imperial Japanese Government; translated by the American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State as enclosure to despatch No. 4324
subfiles.about: The ordinance authorizes centralized control over the generation, distribution, transmission, and consumption of electric power.
subfiles.summary: The Minister of Communications could restrict consumption, suspend or compel supply, direct private and railway generating facilities, order transmission, and require repairs or transfers of electrical equipment. The minister could also determine disputed costs and equipment prices, regulate electricity rates, arrange compensation for losses, and demand reports or inspections. Colonial officials exercised corresponding powers in Chosen, Taiwan, and Karafuto. The ordinance became effective on October 20, 1939 in Japan and October 27 in the named territories.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 6: List of Commodities Prepared by the Central Price Committee
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State as enclosure to despatch No. 4324
subfiles.about: The list identifies imported goods, export commodities, daily necessities, and other important commodities selected for price control.
subfiles.summary: Class I covers imports and goods made from imported materials, including strategic metals, chemicals, textiles, oils, tools, and optical products. Class II lists export goods and daily necessities such as foodstuffs, bicycles, glassware, oils, fertilizers, and household manufactures. Class III includes other important foods, metals, machinery, chemicals, fuels, lumber, agricultural products, and miscellaneous materials, with later additions including oilseeds and grains.
